P4S10 remains spectrally stable up to 130 °C with conserved P]S and P–S vibrational bands (716 and 274 cm−1, panel (a)). figures.caption: Fig. 3 31P and 7Li NMR spectra of thiophosphate reaction products. Panel (a) displays 31P NMR spectra of unﬁltered reaction mixtures, from top to bottom: 1 : 1 Li2S : P4S10 after 2 days, 1 : 1 after 31 days, 2 : 1 after 2 days, 2 : 1 after 31 days, and 2 : 1 after 18 months. Panel (b) presents the corresponding 7Li NMR spectra in the same order. Panel (c) shows expanded regions of the 31P spectra highlighting the observed multiplet splittings for the main resonances. The broken x axis is used only to separate signals for visual clarity; splitting distances are therefore not intended for direct comparison across windows. The 31P observation frequency was 161.9 MHz, and the extracted J values are reported in Hz. Spectra were acquired without 1H decoupling.

Fig. 4 Proposed structural evolution of the Li2S + P4S10 system in acetonitrile up to 2Li2S : 1P4S10 stoichiometry. The schematics show representative candidate structures consistent with the evolution of the thiophosphate framework during reaction and aging. Isomer backbones are highlighted in green and blue for identiﬁcation. Early-stage species are depicted as more open or weakly reorganized structures, while continued rearrangement favors more symmetric candidates. Structures D and E are shown as possible interconverting isomeric forms, with structure E representing the candidate most consistent with the long-time spectroscopic observations; the ﬁnal panel depicts relaxation of the ring form of E. All structures are drawn with lithium and overall charge balance. The schematics are intended for illustrative purposes only; optimized geometries, shielding tensors, energies, and vibratio

Fig. 5 Formally reduced thiophosphate structures considered as possible redox-coupled products. Starting from the P4S10 cage (B) and Li2S, formal reduction generates partially reduced intermediates (CR, formally 2P5+ + 2P4+) and fully reduced isomers. Structures Dr, Er, and Fr are formally 4P4+ interconverting forms; structure Gr, which contains P–P bonds, is formally 4P4+. The connectivity dependence of the formal phosphorus oxidation state (P4+ without P–P bonds versus P4+ with them) illustrates that formal oxidation states are bookkeeping constructs rather than descriptors of the physical electronic structure. These structures are rejected as candidates for the observed solution species and are presented to illustrate possible redox chemistries.

Fig. 6 Rapid reaction of LPSC using stable thiophosphate intermediate. Photographs show the reaction precursors—Li2S in ethanol, LiCl in ethanol, and the thiophosphate intermediate in ACN—prior to mixing (a), and the resulting color change to bluish green after mixing (b). Raman spectroscopy of the 180 °C dried product reveals LPSC-relevant vibrational feature at 426 cm−1 corresponding to PS4 3−(c). XRD patterns (d) of dried and sintered samples are consistent with formation of an LPSC-type argyrodite phase, matching ICSD #418191. Impedance spectroscopy shows high resistance in the dried sample due to grain boundaries (e), while the sintered sample exhibits high ionic conductivity (∼1 mS cm−1) (f).

Fig. 7 STEM-EDX elemental analysis of a particle present in the liquid- phase Li6PS5Cl powder. Elemental maps show phosphorus in blue, sulfur in yellow, and oxygen in red. The P, S, and O signals are spatially distributed across the particle. Quantitative EDX analysis of the agglomerated particles give atomic fractions of 81.70% O, 15.10% P, 2.82% S, and 0.37% Cl, consistent with an oxygen-rich, sulfur/chlorine- depleted agglomerate.

figures.label: S1
figures.caption: Figure S1. Proposed reaction mechanism of Li₂S and P₂S₅ in acetonitrile by Wang et al. The mechanistic pathway presented by Wang et al. involves the stepwise degradation of P₄S₁₀ via nucleophilic attack by Li₂S in acetonitrile, leading to the formation of polyphosphate-like intermediates. The proposed transformations were primarily derived from in situ Raman spectroscopy, with identification of intermediate species based on characteristic vibrational modes and temporal signal evolution. Although not all signals were explicitly assigned, the framework suggests a progression from cage-like P₄S₁₀ to lower- symmetry thiophosphate chains and rings through lithium-mediated cleavage and rearrangement.

figures.label: S2
figures.caption: Figure S2. Proposed reaction mechanism of Li₂S and P₂S₅ in acetonitrile by Calpa et al. Calpa et al. propose a liquid-phase reaction mechanism for the formation of thiophosphate anions during synthesis of sulfide solid electrolytes. Their interpretation is based primarily on ex situ Raman spectroscopy, supplemented by ³¹P NMR, and DFT calculations of vibrational modes. The mechanism suggests progressive cleavage of P–S bonds in P₂S₅ by Li₂S, leading to the formation of linear and branched thiophosphate species with varying chain lengths, such as P₂S₇⁴⁻ and P₃S₉³⁻. Unlike Wang et al., this model emphasizes a more heterogeneous distribution of solution-phase species, without assigning a dominant structural motif.

In the spin density, positive density (blue) localizes on the sulfur atoms, indicating that the unpaired electron resides on the sulfur framework; the smaller opposite-sign density (red) at phosphorus reflects induced spin polarization rather than direct occupation. This localization indicates that one-electron reduction of the thiophosphate unit is sulfur- (ligand-) centered, consistent with the population analysis (Table S11) and the uniform P–S bond elongation. Electron density and spin density plots were generated with OrcaPlot, and the images were rendered in VESTA.

The local 4D-STEM-indexed cell differs from cubic Li6PS5Cl but shows metric similarity to orthorhombic Li3PO4, with smaller cell parameters than the literature values due to the shorter bonds because of oxygen deficiency, supporting the presence of localized phosphate-like domains that may contribute to the reduced effective ionic conductivity of the liquid-phase electrolyte.
